feedback: If a learner thinks 'science has closed the book', note that a genuine minority hypothesis (Deccan volcanism) persists and that the impact case itself strengthened over time as evidence accumulated.

If a learner dismisses the rival outright, ask what the volcanism idea can explain (huge Deccan eruptions happened around the same time and could change the climate) and what evidence would help decide how much each cause mattered.
Affirm reasoning that cites specific converging evidence rather than appealing to who said it.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific knowledge is based on empirical evidence and is provisional: competing hypotheses are judged by how well they explain the evidence, and a genuine rival idea can still have supporters while the main case strengthens.
learnerActions: Compare two explanations for the extinction: the asteroid impact and Deccan Traps volcanism, considering what each can explain and whether both might have played a part.
List which pieces of evidence (worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age crater, iridium inside the crater) fit the impact explanation.
Discuss or write why the impact case grew stronger over decades as new evidence arrived, and why a minority of scientists still support the volcanism idea.

Conclude with a statement about how scientists decide between rival ideas — by how much evidence each explains, not by authority — and that scientific conclusions can be revised as evidence accumulates.
activities.title: Weigh the rival hypothesis

feedback: A strong answer names the global impact winter and food-chain collapse reaching the whole planet, cites the iridium layer and Chicxulub crater, and notes that birds survived.
A partial answer names the asteroid, crater, or iridium layer but explains deaths by the direct blast and cannot describe the worldwide food-chain collapse — redirect to the aftermath activity.
A gap answer pictures the asteroid crushing or burning the dinosaurs with no global mechanism — reteach by separating the local impact from the global after-effects.
On the 'biggest extinction' probe: note that earlier extinctions (End-Permian) killed a far greater share of species; K-Pg is famous, not the largest.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state the age (~66 Mya), name the Chicxulub crater, cite the worldwide iridium layer, order the food-chain-collapse mechanism, and avoid the direct-killing, total-annihilation, and 'biggest-ever' misconceptions.
learnerActions: Put the causal chain in the correct order: impact -> dust cloud -> less sunlight -> photosynthesis crashes -> plants die -> herbivores die -> carnivores die -> ecosystem collapse.

Sort clues into 'impact evidence' (e.g. worldwide iridium layer, shocked quartz, matching-age Chicxulub crater, iridium inside the crater) and items that are NOT impact evidence (e.g. an ordinary dinosaur fossil from older rock, a present-day volcanic rock, a river-worn pebble).
Answer why iridium is a clue (it is rare in Earth's crust but common in asteroids).

Answer the diagnostic question: 'An asteroid hit near Mexico ~66 Mya and most dinosaurs died. Did it kill them all just by crushing or burning them on impact? Explain how a strike in one place could wipe out dinosaurs all over the world.'

Respond to probes such as: since birds are living dinosaurs, is it right to say the asteroid killed ALL the dinosaurs? Why do plant-eaters die before meat-eaters? What evidence shows the effects reached the whole world? Was the K-Pg really the deadliest extinction ever?
activities.title: Check your understanding of the case
